title: Grade 12 Mathematics — Relations and Functions & Inverse Trigonometry
description: Relations and Functions and Inverse Trigonometric Functions practice questions
subject: mathematics

questions.question: A relation R on set A is said to be reflexive if:
options: (a, a) ∈ R for all a ∈ A
(a, b) ∈ R and (b, c) ∈ R implies (a, c) ∈ R
questions.explanation: A relation R on A is reflexive if every element is related to itself: (a, a) ∈ R for all a ∈ A.

questions.question: A function f: A → B is one-one (injective) if:
options: Every element of B has a preimage in A
f is defined for all elements of A
f maps every element of A to the same element in B
questions.explanation: A function is one-one (injective) if distinct inputs give distinct outputs: f(x₁) = f(x₂) ⟹ x₁ = x₂. No two different elements map to the same element.

questions.question: A function f: A → B is onto (surjective) if:
options: Distinct elements of A have distinct images in B
For every b ∈ B, there exists at least one a ∈ A such that f(a) = b
The domain and codomain are the same set
questions.explanation: A function is onto (surjective) if every element in the codomain B is the image of at least one element in the domain A. Range = Codomain.

questions.question: The equivalence relation on Z defined by R = {(a, b) : 2 divides (a − b)} is:
options: Reflexive and symmetric but not transitive
questions.explanation: R is reflexive (a−a=0, divisible by 2), symmetric (if 2|(a−b) then 2|(b−a)), and transitive (if 2|(a−b) and 2|(b−c) then 2|(a−c)). So it is an equivalence relation.

questions.question: The number of bijective functions from a set A with n elements to a set B with n elements is:
questions.explanation: The first element can map to n choices, second to (n−1), and so on. Total bijective functions = n × (n−1) × ... × 1 = n! (n factorial).

questions.question: If f(x) = x² and g(x) = 2x + 1, then fog(x) =
questions.explanation: fog(x) = f(g(x)) = f(2x + 1) = (2x + 1)². The composition applies f after g.

questions.question: The inverse of the function f(x) = 2x + 3 is:
questions.explanation: Let y = 2x + 3. Solve for x: x = (y − 3)/2. So f⁻¹(x) = (x − 3)/2.

questions.question: A relation R on set A is transitive if:
options: (a, b) ∈ R and (b, c) ∈ R ⟹ (a, c) ∈ R
questions.explanation: Transitivity: if (a, b) ∈ R and (b, c) ∈ R, then (a, c) must also be in R. Example: 'is an ancestor of' is transitive.

questions.question: The principal value of sin⁻¹(1/2) is:
questions.explanation: sin⁻¹ has range [−π/2, π/2]. sin(π/6) = 1/2, and π/6 is in [−π/2, π/2]. So sin⁻¹(1/2) = π/6.

questions.question: The domain of cos⁻¹(x) is:
questions.explanation: cos⁻¹(x) is defined for x ∈ [−1, 1], since cosine values lie in [−1, 1]. The range of cos⁻¹ is [0, π].

questions.question: The value of tan⁻¹(1) + tan⁻¹(−1) is:
sin(sin⁻¹(x)) = x is valid for x in:
questions.explanation: sin(sin⁻¹(x)) = x is valid only for x ∈ [−1, 1], which is the domain of sin⁻¹. Outside this range, sin⁻¹(x) is not defined.

questions.question: The value of cos⁻¹(cos(7π/6)) is:
questions.explanation: cos⁻¹(cos θ) = θ only if θ ∈ [0, π]. Since 7π/6 ∉ [0, π], find an equivalent angle: cos(7π/6) = cos(2π − 5π/6) = cos(5π/6) (since cos is even about π: cos(7π/6) = −√3/2 = cos(5π/6)). So cos⁻¹(cos(7π/6)) = 5π/6.

questions.question: tan⁻¹(x) + tan⁻¹(y) = tan⁻¹((x+y)/(1−xy)) is valid when:
questions.explanation: The formula tan⁻¹(x) + tan⁻¹(y) = tan⁻¹((x+y)/(1−xy)) holds when xy < 1. When xy > 1, a correction of ±π is needed.

questions.question: The range of sin⁻¹(x) is:
questions.explanation: sin⁻¹(x) has range [−π/2, π/2] (the principal value branch). cos⁻¹(x) has range [0, π].
